--- PAGE 1 ---
DEVELOPMENT ISSUES IN INDIAN ECONOMY 
NAME OF THE MODULE: Historical Precedents of Development Issues of Indian 
Economy 
TOPIC : Basic Issues in Economic Development 
Objectives 
After studying this topic, students should be able to: 
1. Understand the concept and meaning of economic development.  
2. Differentiate between economic growth and economic development.  
3. Identify the major issues and challenges faced by developing economies.  
4. Explain the problems of poverty, unemployment, and inequality in the development 
process.  
5. Analyze the causes and consequences of low productivity and low income levels.  
 Introduction 
Economic development is a broad and complex process that goes beyond mere economic growth 
or increase in national income. It involves structural transformation, improvement in living 
standards, reduction of poverty, and enhancement of human well-being. These challenges are 
referred to as the basic issues in economic development. 
Basic issues in economic development arise mainly because resources are limited while human 
needs are unlimited. Developing economies, in particular, struggle with problems such as 
poverty, unemployment, income inequality, low productivity, population growth, regional 
imbalances, and inadequate infrastructure. These issues prevent the equitable distribution of 
wealth and restrict opportunities for large sections of society. As a result, economic growth may 
not translate into improved quality of life for all citizens. 
Poverty as a Basic Issue in Economic Development  
Poverty is one of the most fundamental and persistent issues in economic development, 
especially in developing and underdeveloped countries. It refers to a condition in which 
individuals or groups lack sufficient income and resources to meet their basic needs of life, such 
as food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, and education. Poverty is not only an economic problem 
but also a social and human issue, as it affects dignity, opportunities, and overall quality of life. 
Despite economic growth in many nations, poverty continues to exist due to unequal distribution 
of income and limited access to essential services. 
Poverty has multiple causes and is often the result of a combination of economic, social, and 
institutional factors. Unemployment and underemployment are major contributors, as lack of 
stable income limits purchasing power and consumption. Low productivity in agriculture, 
especially in rural areas, keeps incomes low and perpetuates rural poverty. Rapid population 

--- PAGE 2 ---
growth also increases pressure on limited resources and employment opportunities. 
Additionally, lack of education and skills restricts access to better-paying jobs, creating a cycle 
of poverty that passes from one generation to the next. Social discrimination, gender inequality, 
and regional disparities further intensify the problem. 
The consequences of poverty are wide-ranging and deeply interconnected. Poor households often 
suffer from malnutrition, poor health, illiteracy, and inadequate housing, which reduce their 
capacity to work productively and escape poverty. Children from impoverished families may 
drop out of school early to support household income, limiting their future opportunities. Poverty 
also contributes to social problems such as crime, migration, and political instability, thereby 
slowing overall economic development. 
Governments attempt to reduce poverty through poverty alleviation programmes, employment 
schemes, subsidies, public distribution systems, and social welfare policies. Investments in 
education, healthcare, skill development, and infrastructure are essential for breaking the cycle of 
poverty. Inclusive economic growth that generates employment and ensures equitable 
distribution of resources is considered the most effective long-term solution. 
In conclusion, poverty remains a central challenge in economic development because it directly 
affects human well-being and social stability. Eliminating poverty requires coordinated efforts in 
economic planning, social justice, and human capital development. True development can be 
achieved only when economic growth leads to improved living standards and equal opportunities 
for all sections of society. 
Unemployment as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Unemployment is one of the most serious and persistent problems faced by developing as well as 
developed economies. It refers to a situation in which people who are willing, able, and actively 
seeking work are unable to find suitable employment at the prevailing wage rate. In the context 
of economic development, unemployment is not merely a labour market issue; it is a structural 
and social challenge that directly affects income levels, productivity, poverty, and overall 
national progress. 
Economic development aims at improving living standards, increasing income, and ensuring 
productive use of resources. However, when a large section of the population remains 
unemployed or underemployed, the economy fails to utilise its human resources effectively. 
Labour is one of the most important factors of production, and unemployment leads to wastage 
of this valuable resource. As a result, national income and output remain below potential, 
slowing economic growth and development. 
Unemployment in developing countries often takes multiple forms such as open unemployment, 
disguised unemployment, seasonal unemployment, and educated unemployment. Open 
unemployment is visible, where individuals are completely without jobs despite actively 
searching for work. Disguised unemployment, common in agriculture, occurs when more 
workers are engaged than required, resulting in very low or zero marginal productivity. Seasonal 
unemployment arises in sectors like agriculture and tourism where work is available only during 

--- PAGE 3 ---
certain times of the year. Educated unemployment reflects the mismatch between educational 
qualifications and job opportunities, especially among youth. 
The causes of unemployment are diverse and interconnected. Rapid population growth,,, slow 
industrialisation,,, technological changes,,, inadequate skill development,,, and poor planning 
contribute significantly to the problem. In many developing economies, dependence on 
agriculture with low productivity and limited non-farm opportunities further intensifies 
unemployment. Structural imbalances between rural and urban sectors also create unequal 
employment opportunities. 
The consequences of unemployment extend beyond economics. It leads to poverty, income 
inequality, social unrest, crime, migration, and psychological stress. Families without stable 
income struggle to access education, healthcare, and decent living conditions, creating a cycle of 
deprivation that passes across generations. From a macroeconomic perspective, high 
unemployment reduces aggregate demand, lowers tax revenue, and increases government 
expenditure on welfare schemes. 
In conclusion, unemployment is a fundamental barrier to economic development because it 
represents both economic inefficiency and social injustice. True development can be achieved 
only when the workforce is productively engaged, income opportunities are widely available, 
and growth translates into meaningful employment for all sections of society. 
Income Inequality as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Income inequality refers to the unequal distribution of income and wealth among individuals or 
groups within an economy. It is a major issue in economic development because growth in 
national income does not automatically ensure that the benefits of development reach all sections 
of society. When income is concentrated in the hands of a small percentage of the population 
while a large majority earns very little, the result is economic imbalance and social injustice. 
In many developing countries, rapid economic growth often coexists with high levels of 
inequality. This happens because certain sectors, regions, or skilled groups benefit more from 
economic expansion than others. Urban areas may grow faster than rural regions, and industries 
may offer higher wages compared to agriculture. As a result, disparities arise between rich and 
poor, urban and rural populations, skilled and unskilled workers, and different social groups. 
The causes of income inequality are multifaceted. Unequal access to education and skills, 
unemployment, regional disparities, technological change, and inheritance of wealth are major 
contributors. Globalisation and market-oriented reforms sometimes widen inequality because 
high-skill sectors grow faster than labour-intensive ones. Social discrimination based on caste, 
gender, or ethnicity can also limit opportunities for certain groups, reinforcing unequal income 
patterns. 
The consequences of income inequality are significant for economic development. High 
inequality can lead to poverty, social unrest, reduced social mobility, and political instability. It 
weakens aggregate demand because lower-income groups have limited purchasing power. 

--- PAGE 4 ---
Inequality can also restrict human capital formation, as poorer families may not afford quality 
education and healthcare, thereby perpetuating the cycle of deprivation across generations. 
Excessive inequality undermines the principle of inclusive growth and reduces the overall 
effectiveness of development policies. 
Governments attempt to reduce income inequality through progressive taxation, social welfare 
programmes, minimum wage laws, public expenditure on education and healthcare, land 
reforms, and employment generation schemes. Policies promoting financial inclusion, skill 
development, and equal opportunities also play a crucial role in narrowing income gaps. 
In conclusion, income inequality is a critical challenge in economic development because it 
affects both economic efficiency and social equity. Sustainable development requires not only 
growth in national income but also fair and equitable distribution of resources and opportunities. 
An economy can be considered truly developed only when prosperity is shared widely and all 
citizens have the chance to improve their standard of living 
Population Pressure as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Population pressure refers to the situation in which the size of a country’s population grows 
faster than the availability of resources, employment opportunities, and infrastructure needed to 
support it. It is a significant issue in economic development, particularly in developing countries 
where high birth rates and declining death rates lead to rapid population growth. When 
population increases beyond the economy’s capacity to provide adequate food, housing, 
education, healthcare, and jobs, it creates serious economic and social challenges. 
In theory, population can be an asset because a larger workforce has the potential to increase 
production and economic growth. However, when growth is uncontrolled or unplanned, it 
becomes a burden rather than a benefit. Excess population places heavy pressure on natural 
resources such as land, water, forests, and energy. Agricultural land gets fragmented, urban areas 
become overcrowded, and environmental degradation intensifies. This reduces productivity and 
slows economic progress. 
One of the major consequences of population pressure is unemployment and underemployment. 
When the labour force grows faster than job creation, many people remain unemployed or work 
in low-paid informal jobs. This leads to poverty, low income levels, and poor living standards. 
Rapid population growth also increases dependency ratios, meaning a smaller working 
population must support a larger non-working population, including children and the elderly. 
This weakens savings and investment capacity in the economy. 
Population pressure also affects social infrastructure and public services. Governments struggle 
to provide quality education, healthcare, housing, sanitation, and transportation to a rapidly 
expanding population. Schools become overcrowded, hospitals are overstretched, and urban 
slums expand. Limited access to these basic services reduces human capital formation and 
restricts long-term development prospects. 

--- PAGE 5 ---
To address population pressure, governments adopt measures such as family planning 
programmes, awareness campaigns, women’s education, delayed marriage, and improved 
healthcare. Education and empowerment of women play a crucial role in reducing fertility rates. 
At the same time, economic policies that create employment opportunities and improve 
productivity can convert a large population into a demographic dividend rather than a liability. 
In conclusion, population pressure becomes a basic issue in economic development when growth 
is not matched with adequate resources, employment, and infrastructure. Balanced population 
growth combined with effective planning, education, and economic expansion can transform 
population from a burden into a powerful driver of national development. 
Infrastructure Deficit as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Infrastructure deficit refers to the shortage or inadequacy of basic physical and social facilities 
required for economic and social activities in a country. Infrastructure includes transport (roads, 
railways, ports, airports), power supply, communication networks, irrigation systems, healthcare, 
education, sanitation, and digital connectivity. When these essential facilities are insufficient, 
outdated, or unevenly distributed, it creates a major obstacle to economic development. 
Infrastructure acts as the backbone of an economy because it supports production, trade, 
mobility, and human welfare. Industries require reliable electricity, good transportation, and 
communication systems to operate efficiently. Farmers need irrigation facilities and storage 
systems to increase agricultural productivity. Similarly, education and healthcare infrastructure 
are necessary for human capital formation. Without adequate infrastructure, even abundant 
natural and human resources cannot be effectively utilised. 
The consequences of infrastructure deficit are widespread. It results in low productivity, high 
transaction costs, reduced competitiveness, and slow economic growth. Socially, poor 
infrastructure leads to limited access to education, healthcare, clean water, and sanitation, which 
lowers the standard of living and worsens inequality. Infrastructure gaps also discourage foreign 
direct investment because investors prefer regions with stable and efficient facilities. 
Another important aspect is the link between infrastructure and regional development. When 
infrastructure is concentrated in certain areas, migration towards cities increases, causing urban 
overcrowding and slum formation while rural regions remain underdeveloped. This imbalance 
creates long-term social and economic disparities within the country. 
Governments address infrastructure deficits through public investment, public–private 
partnerships (PPP), foreign investment, and policy reforms. Large-scale projects in 
transportation, renewable energy, digital connectivity, smart cities, and rural development aim to 
bridge these gaps. Efficient governance, transparency, and long-term planning are essential to 
ensure infrastructure development is sustainable and inclusive. 
In conclusion, infrastructure deficit is a critical barrier to economic development because it 
restricts productivity, investment, and human welfare. Strong and well-planned infrastructure not 
only accelerates economic growth but also improves quality of life and promotes balanced 

--- PAGE 6 ---
regional development. Therefore, infrastructure development is considered a strategic 
foundation for sustainable and inclusive economic progress. 
Environmental Issues as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Environmental issues have emerged as one of the most critical challenges in modern economic 
development. While economic growth aims at increasing production, income, and living 
standards, it often leads to the excessive use of natural resources and environmental degradation. 
When development activities harm air, water, land, forests, and biodiversity, the long-term 
sustainability of growth becomes threatened. Therefore, environmental protection has become an 
integral part of development planning. 
Economic development traditionally focused on industrialisation, urbanisation, and infrastructure 
expansion without giving adequate attention to environmental consequences. This approach 
resulted in problems such as pollution, deforestation, climate change, soil erosion, water 
scarcity, and loss of biodiversity. Developing countries, in their pursuit of rapid growth, 
frequently face a trade-off between economic expansion and environmental conservation. 
However, ignoring environmental costs eventually reduces productivity and quality of life. 
One of the major environmental issues is pollution—air, water, and soil pollution caused by 
industries, vehicles, and improper waste management. Air pollution leads to respiratory diseases 
and reduced labour productivity. Water pollution affects drinking water quality, agriculture, and 
aquatic life. Similarly, land degradation and deforestation reduce agricultural output and increase 
vulnerability to natural disasters such as floods and landslides. 
Another significant concern is climate change, driven by greenhouse gas emissions from fossil 
fuels and industrial activities. Rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall, droughts, and extreme 
weather events directly affect agriculture, food security, and livelihoods, especially in developing 
economies dependent on natural resources. Environmental degradation also increases healthcare 
costs and reduces economic efficiency. 
Environmental issues are closely linked to poverty and inequality. Poor communities often 
depend heavily on natural resources for survival and are the most affected by environmental 
damage. Lack of clean water, sanitation, and safe living conditions worsens their economic 
situation, creating a vicious cycle between poverty and environmental decline. 
To address these challenges, the concept of sustainable development has gained importance. 
Sustainable development emphasises meeting present needs without compromising the ability of 
future generations to meet their own needs. Governments and international organisations 
promote policies such as renewable energy adoption, afforestation, pollution control laws, waste 
management systems, green technologies, and environmental awareness programmes. Balancing 
economic growth with environmental conservation is now considered essential for long-term 
prosperity. 
In conclusion, environmental issues are a fundamental concern in economic development 
because they directly affect human health, productivity, and resource availability. Development 

--- PAGE 7 ---
that ignores environmental sustainability may yield short-term gains but leads to long-term 
losses. Therefore, integrating environmental protection with economic planning ensures 
inclusive, balanced, and sustainable growth for present and future generations. 
Regional Imbalance as a Basic Issue in Economic Development 
Regional imbalance refers to the unequal development of different regions within a country. It 
occurs when certain areas, often urban or industrially advanced regions, experience rapid 
economic growth and high standards of living, while others, typically rural or resource-poor 
areas, lag behind. This uneven growth creates disparities in income, employment opportunities, 
infrastructure, social services, and overall quality of life. Regional imbalance is a critical issue in 
economic development because it hampers equitable growth and social cohesion. 
Causes of Regional Imbalance 
Several factors contribute to regional disparities in developing economies: 
1. Uneven Resource Distribution: Natural resources like fertile land, water, minerals, and 
energy sources are not evenly distributed. Regions rich in resources tend to attract 
investment, industries, and infrastructure development, while resource-poor areas are 
neglected 
2. Concentration of Industries and Urbanization: Industrial development is often 
concentrated in a few urban or metropolitan regions due to better infrastructure, skilled 
labour, and market access. Rural regions or backward areas are left out of industrial 
growth, leading to income and employment gaps 
3. Infrastructure Gaps: Differences in transport, communication, electricity, and digital 
connectivity across regions affect investment and productivity. Well-connected regions 
grow faster, while poorly connected areas remain underdeveloped 
4. Historical and Policy Factors: Colonial legacy, past administrative focus, and policy 
decisions often favored certain regions, creating historical inequalities. Lack of targeted 
development policies for backward regions exacerbates these imbalances 
5. Human Capital Disparities: Unequal access to education, healthcare, and skill 
development contributes to regional differences. Regions with better human capital 
attract investment and generate higher incomes, while others struggle with poverty and 
unemployment 
Consequences of Regional Imbalance 
Regional imbalance has far-reaching economic, social, and political consequences: 
 
Economic Consequences: It leads to inefficient use of resources, underemployment, low 
productivity, and slower national growth. Backward regions fail to contribute optimally 
to the economy 
 
Social Consequences: Disparities in income, education, and health increase social 
tensions and migration pressures. People from backward regions migrate to developed 

--- PAGE 8 ---
areas in search of employment, causing urban overcrowding, slums, and pressure on civic 
amenities 
 
Political Consequences: Regional disparities may lead to feelings of neglect and 
marginalization, creating political unrest, demands for autonomy, or separatist 
movements in extreme cases 
Policy Measures to Reduce Regional Imbalance 
Governments and planners adopt several measures to reduce regional disparities: 
1. Balanced Regional Development: Promoting industrialization, infrastructure, and 
services in backward areas through incentives, subsidies, and special economic zones 
2. Investment in Human Capital: Establishing schools, vocational training centres, and 
healthcare facilities in lagging regions to improve productivity and employability 
3. Fiscal and Financial Measures: Allocating funds through central transfers, development 
grants, and targeted welfare programmes to uplift backward regions 
4. Decentralisation and Local Governance: Empowering local governments to plan and 
implement region-specific development initiatives ensures better resource utilization 
5. Infrastructure Development: Improving transport, power, and digital connectivity to 
attract investment and integrate backward regions with the mainstream economy 
Conclusion 
Regional imbalance is a critical barrier to inclusive and sustainable economic development. 
Unequal growth across regions not only reduces national productivity but also perpetuates 
poverty, unemployment, and social inequality. Addressing regional disparities requires strategic 
planning, targeted investment, human capital development, and equitable distribution of 
resources. A country can achieve true development only when all regions progress together, 
ensuring balanced growth, social harmony, and economic stability. 
MCQ 
1. Which of the following is considered a hidden form of unemployment common in 
agriculture? 
A) Open unemployment 
B) Seasonal unemployment 
C) Disguised unemployment 
D) Educated unemployment 
Answer: C) Disguised unemployment 
2. Income inequality can hinder economic development because: 
A) It always increases national income 
B) It reduces aggregate demand and social cohesion 
C) It guarantees equitable access to resources 
D) It encourages industrial growth 

--- PAGE 9 ---
Answer: B) It reduces aggregate demand and social cohesion 
3. Population pressure becomes a problem when: 
A) Labour force is adequately employed 
B) Population grows faster than available resources and infrastructure 
C) Urban areas are well-planned 
D) Birth and death rates are equal 
Answer: B) Population grows faster than available resources and infrastructure 
4. Which of the following is an example of infrastructure deficit? 
A) Unequal income distribution 
B) Lack of sufficient roads, electricity, and hospitals 
C) High inflation rate 
D) Seasonal unemployment 
Answer: B) Lack of sufficient roads, electricity, and hospitals 
5. Regional imbalance in economic development refers to: 
A) Equal income levels across all regions 
B) Unequal growth and development between regions 
C) Shortage of natural resources 
D) High population density 
Answer: B) Unequal growth and development between regions

                                                      MODULE I:    
HISTORICAL PRECEDENTS OF DEVELOPMENT ISSUES OF INDAIN ECONOMY  
           The Indian economy is, at present, undergoing far – reaching changes, as it moves from 
the state of underdevelopment to development. in this phase of transition, it has much to its 
credit, and is, at the same time, beset with many problems. To understand all this, we first 
discuss as a background, and we elaborate upon the theme of development to know about the 
ways whereby an underdeveloped economy transforms itself into a developed economy. By 
understanding the phenomenon of underdevelopment, it is useful for understanding the 
problems faced by India during its development process. This will help us in identifying the 
underdeveloped countries and in recognizing the gravity of the problem these countries face. 
This will also provide us a perspective to oversee India’s placing in the overall context of the 
underdeveloped world.   
By studying this chapter students will be able to understand  
➢ Difference between economic development and economic growth 
➢ The development issues existed in past Indian economy  
➢ Provide basic understanding about how they overcome development issues in Indian 
economy.  
 
Economic Growth implies the change in per capita income, while economic development 
means economic growth plus change. Change here may be welfare changes or distributional 
changes. 
➢ Features of Modern Economic Growth; given by Kuznets: 
▪ High rates of growth per capita product (10 times) and population (5 times). 
▪ Rise in productivity 
▪ High Rate of Structural Transformation: Shift away from agriculture to non-agricultural 
sectors. 
▪ Increased urbanisation 
➢ Economic development: - features 
▪ Process: Social (Control of population), technological (new technology) or economic 
forces (efficient use of resources). 
▪ Real National Income: Positive relationship between Real National Income and Economic 
development Stability of price is an essential condition for promoting development.  
▪  Long period: Real national should continue to rise in long run. Accelerates development. 
➢ Amartya Sen’s Concept of Development:  
▪ He gave the concept in 1980s in his work “Development as Freedom”. 

--- PAGE 2 ---
▪ According to him, development would mean if there is:  
▪ Capabilities to function: Entitlements give a right in the society, which further decides 
their capabilities to function. 
▪ Included freedom: Principal means of achieving development/ Removing un-freedoms 
like lack of political freedom, famine and under-nourishment) 
▪  Dudley Seers, in his work “The Meaning of Development” (1969), took three indicators 
which would reflect whether development has occurred or not. The indicators are: 
▪ Unemployment 
▪ Poverty 
▪ Inequality 
▪ Decline in any of them would lead to development 
▪ Denis Goulet introduced three core values of development in his work “The Cruel Choice: 
A New Concept in the Theory of Development” which are:  
▪ Life sustenance: Ability of a person to meet his basic needs, which can be in the form of 
reduction in absolute poverty, hunger, etc.  
▪ Self-Esteem: Ability to be a person, that is, kind of things a person enjoys like self-esteem, 
dignity, etc. In other words, there should not be a feeling of inferiority complex.  
▪ Freedom: Freedom from servitude, person should be free from miseries, exploitation, etc.  
Characteristics of an Under-Developed Economy: 
▪ General Poverty 
▪ Dualistic economy 
▪ Demographic features 
▪ Economic backwardness 
▪ Agriculture: Main occupation 
▪ Under-developed natural resources 
▪ Unemployment and disguised unemployment 
▪ Lack of enterprise and initiative 
▪ Insufficient capital equipment 
▪ Foreign trade orientation  
▪ Technological backwardness  
 
 
 
▪ Amartya Sen was the major contributor in the concept of Sustainable Development. The 
concept appeared in 1987 in “Our Common Future: The Brundtland Report”.  
▪ Sustainable development: Meeting the needs of present generation without compromising 
the needs of future generation.  
▪ To promote the concept of sustainable development, Ministry of Environment and Forests 
(MOEF) was set up in India in 1985. 

--- PAGE 3 ---
▪ It is obvious that the salvation of an underdeveloped economy lies in its development. 
We, therefore, enlarge upon the theme of development in this chapter. This we do by 
taking up first the meaning and indicators of development. For a neat analysis of the 
problems of underdeveloped economy we have to know What is mean by development: 
in the context of the underdeveloped countries like India, development is defined as a 
sustained increase in the real per capita income together with an improvement in the 
distribution of material welfare. This definition involves advancement on two aspects of 
economic life, namely, income and distribution.  As per income the focus is on the rise in 
the per capita income. this requires a growth rate which is higher than the rate of increase 
in population. Since the population growth is quite high in the range of two or three per 
cent, and the income levels very low in these countries, the growth rate of national income 
has to be sufficiently large to make any significant impact on the dismal income – 
situation.  It is also necessary that the rise in the per capita income should be a sustained 
one. In other words, the rise should continue over a long period , spread over several 
decades. Further, the rise in the percapita income must be in real terms. This requires that 
the rise in the money income should be higher than rise in the price level. it is only then 
that, on an average, more goods and services will become available. 
▪ In the context of the definition of development, it may be useful to refer to the concept of 
sustainable development which is now in common use.  
▪ Definition: Sustainable development is defined as meeting the needs of the present 
without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. 
▪ Three Pillars: It rests on economic, social, and environmental pillars. 
▪ Key Principles: Important principles include intergenerational equity, integrating 
environmental and economic goals, social inclusion, the precautionary principle, and the 
polluter pays principle.  
➢ The 17 SDGs were adopted by the UN in 2015 to provide a global framework. They 
are:  
▪ No poverty 
▪ Zero hunger 
▪ Good health and well being 
▪ Quality education 
▪ Gender equality 
▪ Clean water and sanitation 
▪ Affordable and clean energy 
▪ Decent work and economic growth 
▪ industry, innovation and infrastructure 
▪ Sustainable cities and communities 
▪ Reduced inequality  

--- PAGE 4 ---
▪ Responsible consumption and production 
▪ Climate action 
▪ Life below water 
▪ Life on land 
▪ Peace, justice and strong institutions Partnerships for the goals 
▪ Global initiatives and frameworks 
Significant initiatives include the Brundtland Report (1987) which introduced the concept, 
the Rio Earth Summit (1992) resulting in Agenda 21, the Millennium Development Goals 
(MDGs), the Paris Agreement (2015), and various conventions like the Ramsar Convention, 
Montreal Protocol, and the Convention on Biological Diversity.  
India's progress, challenges, and initiatives:  
 
▪ NITI Aayog's SDG India Index: This index tracks state and UT performance on the 
SDGs. 
▪ Government Initiatives: Schemes like Swachh Bharat Mission and the National Solar 
Mission are examples of India's efforts. 
▪ Challenges: India faces challenges including resource limitations, inequality, 
environmental degradation, and implementation issues. 
▪ Strategies: Strengthening data, improving governance, SDG-based budgeting, and 
public participation are key strategies. 
▪ The concept of sustainable development, while formally defined in the late 20th 
century, has roots that extend back further. Its origins can be understood by tracing the 
evolution of concerns about the relationship between human actions, economic growth, 
and the environment.  
 
➢ Here's a look at the historical development of the concept: 
 
Early ideas about sustainable resource management, particularly in forestry, emerged in 
Europe during the 17th and 18th centuries due to concerns about timber depletion. Later, 
environmentalists like John Muir and Rachel Carson raised awareness about the impact 
of industrialization on nature, while social thinkers highlighted societal inequalities. 
Although the post-World War II era focused on economic growth, the negative 
environmental and social consequences, such as the Great Smog of London and the issues 
highlighted in Rachel Carson's "Silent Spring," became apparent. In the mid-20th century, 
there was a growing recognition of the need to integrate economic systems with ecological 
limitations.  
        Formal emergence (1970s-1980s) 
The connection between sustainability and development became more explicit in the early 
1970s. The "Limits to Growth" report in 1972 warned about the potential consequences 
of continued economic and population growth. The 1972 United Nations Conference on 

--- PAGE 5 ---
the Human Environment (Stockholm Conference) was a key event that focused on the 
link between development and the environment. The term "sustainable development" was 
introduced in the 1980 World Conservation Strategy. However, the 1987 Brundtland 
Report, "Our Common Future," significantly popularized the term and provided its widely 
accepted definition: "Development that meets the needs of the present without 
compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".  
Global recognition and frameworks (1990s - present) 
▪ The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro built upon the Brundtland Report and 
established a global framework for sustainable development, emphasizing the integration 
of environmental, social, and economic factors. While the Millennium Development 
Goals (MDGs) addressed poverty, they were criticized for not fully integrating 
environmental sustainability. In 2015, the United Nations adopted the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs) as part of the 2030 Agenda, which are universal and cover a 
broad range of interconnected social, economic, and environmental targets.  
▪ In essence, sustainable development emerged from a growing awareness of the negative 
impacts of unchecked economic growth on the environment and society, highlighting the 
need to balance these factors for present and future well-being.  
 
▪ When economic development take place, investment increases and the stock of capital 
increases. 
▪ When total output increases, per capita consumption may increase or decrease 
▪ Some economists suggest that economic growth and economic development means an 
increase in quantitative aspects such as total output. 
▪ Qualitative measures such as education standard of living are also included by some other 
economists to measure the economic growth or development. 
▪ Different viewpoints are there to measure the growth and development. 
 
                              OLD INDEX FOR MEASURING DEVELOPMENT  
 
1)National income as an index 
▪ An increase in real national income is the most convenient measure of economic 
development because a larger real national income is normally a pre-requisite for an 
increase in real per capita (Kuznets, Meier and Baldwin)  
▪ But the use of national income as an index to measure economic development has been 
criticizes due to aggregative grounds. 
▪ It ignored the consumption and distribution of resources 
▪ It does not account for population trends as does per capita income. 
2) Per capita income as an index 
▪ Population is an important concern of economic development 
▪ Increase in national income should be greater than the rate of growth of population 

--- PAGE 6 ---
▪ In developing countries having population pressure a rise in per capita real income is 
better than that of aggregate real income in the measurement of economic development. 
3) Per capita level of consumption 
▪ Increase in per capita income need not always increase per capita consumption which 
affect the standard of living of the people. 
▪ Improving the standard of living of the people is the ultimate objective of economic 
development. then the per capita consumption level is the most appropriate index of 
measuring economic development. 
UNRISD Indicator of socio- economic development United Nations Research Institute for 
Social Development tried to develop such indices as would encompass social, political and 
economic variables related to industrialisation, urbanisation and modernisation. 
 
                
 
 
1)Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)  
▪ It was developed for the Overseas Development Council in the mid 1970 by Morris 
David Morris, as one of a number of measures created due to dissatisfaction with 
the use of GNP as an indicator of development. 
▪ He used three important indicators 
• Life Expectancy (LE) 
• Infant Mortality (IM) 
• Basic Literacy (BL) 
▪ Morris suggested that since infant mortality refers to death before age one , therefore 
life expectancy at age one should be used instead of life expectancy at birth. 
▪ These three indicators are averaged to get PQLI i.e , 
        PQLI= 1/3 (LEI + IM + BL) 
2)Human Development Index  
▪ The Human Development Index (HDI) is a static composite index of life 
expectancy, education and per capita income indicators, which are used to rank 
countries into four tiers of human development. 
▪ The index was developed in 1990 by Indian Nobel Prize Winner Amartya Sen and 
Pakistani economist Mahbub Ul Haq, with help from Gustav Ranis of yale 
University and Lord Meghnad Desai of the London school of Economics and has 
been used since by the United Nations Development Program in its annual Human 
Development Report. 
  Components of HDI: 
▪ HDI Comprises of three main components 

--- PAGE 7 ---
➢ Life Expectancy Index (LEI): It is the life expectancy at birth, not at age one because 
infant mortality   is not entering in this index as a separate indicator. 
➢ Educational Attainment Index (EAI): It is a combination of adult literacy rate with 
2/3 weight and combined enrolment ratio with weight 1/3 
➢ Standard of living index (SLI): It is represented here by a transformation of per 
incomes are converted into purchasing power parity (PPP).  Presently standard of 
living is being captured by the long transform of per capita income in PPP. 
▪ HDI is an Equi – weighted average of above three components. i.e 
              HDI= 1/3 (LEI + EAI+ SLI) 
▪ The geometric mean of the three indexes the cube root of the product of the indexes is 
the human development index.  
▪ A value above 0.800 is classified as very high between 0.700 and 0.799 high, 0.550 to 
0.699 as medium and anything below 0.550 as low. 
3) Poverty Index 
▪ The Human Poverty Index (HPI) was an indication of the poverty of community in a 
country, developed by the United Nations to complement the Human Development 
Index (HDI) and was first reported as part of the Human Deprivation Report in 1997. 
▪ While the HDI measures average achievement, the HPI measures deprivations in the 
three base dimensions of human development captured in HDI.  
➢ A long and a healthy life 
➢ Knowledge  
➢ A decent standard of living 
4)Gender Development Index 
▪ The Gender Development Index (GDI) is an index designed to measure gender 
equality. 
▪ GDI together with the Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM) were introduced in 
1995 in the Human Development Report written by the United Nations 
Development Program.  
▪ The aim of this measurement was to add a gender- sensitive dimension to the 
Human Development Index (HDI)  
▪ The GDI adjusts the average achievements to reflect the inequalities between men 
and women in the following dimensions. 
➢ A long and a healthy life 
➢ Knowledge 
➢ A decent standard of living 
▪ Gender Development Index based on data collected in 2018 and published in 2019 
▪ Countries are grouped into five groups based on the absolute deviation from gender 
parity in HDI values from 1 (closest to gender parity) to 5 (further from gender parity). 
This means that grouping takes equally into consideration gender gaps favouring males 
as well as those favouring females.  
  

--- PAGE 8 ---
      5)   Social Progress Indicate 
▪ SPI refers to social progress defined at the individual level in three dimensions. 
▪ These three dimensions are 
➢ Longevity or potential lifetime 
➢ Consumption of private goods  
➢ Access to public goods 
▪ The index is published by the nonprofit social progress imperative and is based on the 
writings of Amartya Sen, Douglas North, and Joseph Stiglitz. 
 
6)  Genuine Progress Indicator 
▪ Genuine progress indicator is a metric that has been suggested to replace or supplement 
gross domestic product (GDP)  
▪ The GDI is designed to take fuller account of the well-being of a nation only a part of 
which pertains to the size of the nation’s economy by incorporating environmental and 
social factors which are not measured by GDP. 
▪ GPI includes more than 20 aspects of our economic life that the GDP ignores. 
▪ The value of activities that add to human progress are added and those which reduce 
progress are subtracted from the measure. 
7) Green Index 
▪ The world banks environmentally sustainable development division has developed 
a new index called Green Index. 
▪ The Green index attaches a dollar value to each of the three components  
➢ Produced assets 
➢ Natural resources  
➢ Human resources 
▪ It puts a price tag on polluted assets the sum of all machineries factories roads and other 
infrastructure 
▪ It then calculates the true estimate of a country’s wealth taking into account all such 
resources which do not always show up on traditional economic indicators. 
7) Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 
▪ The multidimensional poverty index was launched by the UNDP and the OPHI in 
2010. 
▪ MPI is based on the idea that poverty is not unidimensional (not just depends on 
income and one individual may lack several basic needs like education, health etc.) 
rather it is multidimensional.  
▪ The index shows the proportion of poor people and the average number of 
deprivations each poor person experiences at the same time. 
▪ MPI uses three dimensions and ten indicators which are:

POLITICAL FACTOR: Colonialism 
Perhaps the greatest single factor which has obstructed the development of many of these 
countries is political in nature. These countries until recently were under the political 
domination of foreign rule. Till as recently as the late forties of this century the economic life 
of these countries was yoked to the needs and compulsions of foreign rulers. Although most of 
these countries have secured independence beginning with 1945, these have not as yet shed 
completely the shackles of a dependent country. For example, they have not totally freed 
themselves externally from the politics of the industrialized nations and internally from the 
hangover of the past regimes. 
Draining surplus: An important way the foreign rulers prevented the development of these 
countries was by draining them of their surpluses. These were sucked through various devices:  
very high payments to foreigners for their work, service personal etc.; such as home charges 
(i.e , interest, pensions etc. to UK) paid by India to England. 
Market for manufactures and sources for raw materials: The colonial countries also 
exploited the markets to their advantage. They took hold of raw materials and food grains for 
their industries and labor.  
Slow capital- intensive modernization: there was then slow growth of capital-intensive 
modern sector. Sponsored largely by the foreigners, the modern sector remained confined to 
such areas as plantations, minerals and mining. these were however looked upon as sources of 
exports only the foreigners. A few capital-intensive projects to lay down railways were also 
undertaken. but these too remained small as these were meant only to serve the limited needs 
of trade for moving agricultural products from the interior of these countries to ports and 
imported manufactured products from the parts to the interior of these countries. No efforts 
were made to expand these sectors to overshadow the domestic traditional industries.

How economies grow and change: 
For an underdeveloped economy to develop two things must happen. One, its output should 
grow over a long period. Two, its economic structure should change to acquire the 
characteristics of developed countries such as an increase in the contributions of industries to 
the economy’s total output. It is this growth plus change that constitutes development.  
Forces of growth 
   The forces that increase output are associated with such factors as capital technology and 
human skills. To understand the growth process, we may analyze the way these factors operate 
to increase the output and how the increase is sustained over a long period. To explain and 
illustrate this we may take up the case of a typical underdeveloped economy. Such an economy 
has natural resources largely land that are fixed in quantity. It has simple and few pieces of 
capital equipment. Its technology is given and is largely primitive. Its human resources consist 
of a large quantity of labor, mostly unskilled.  
Operation of diminishing returns 
In this state of affairs, an increase in output can take place only with an increase in all the 
factors of production. Since with given technology these factors are combined in a certain 
proportion, an increase in them should take place in that proportion. roughly one can say that 
if all these factors are doubled, output will double. But it should be noted that with the doubling 
of labor, output per worker remains the same despite doubling of the total output.  
     But it is extraordinarily difficult to expand all the factors in a proportionate way. For 
example, it is not possible to increase land as per our needs it is fixed. in our economy capital 
stock too is fixed. in our economy capital stock too is fixed. And so is technology. The only 

--- PAGE 29 ---
factor which let us suppose can increase is the quantity of labor. If equal doses of labor are 
increasingly applied to fixed land and capital the output will become subject to diminishing 
returns. That is the increase in output will be at a diminishing rate. This is because each worker 
will be equipped with smaller amounts of land and capital. In other words, more laborers will 
be farming each acre of land, and each laborer will have fewer tools to work with. Thus, as a 
result of diminishing products the total product will rise slowly. After a point, however, the 
increase in marginal product becomes less than the average product. This not only reduces the 
total product but also the average productivity or per capita product of the worker. Thus, both 
in terms of total product and per capita product the economy takes a downward turn.  
OVERCOMING GROWTH HURDLES  
An increase in capital stock, an advance in technology and an improvement in the skill of labor 
can offset or forestall diminishing returns. As a result, a larger output an take place and higher 
productivity per worker can be achieved. With every given progress in the factors of 
production, total product and productivity per worker having risen will again be subject to 
diminishing returns. But every time this happens the growth – forces will postpone their full 
operation. This happens because the very assumptions or conditions of the law of diminishing 
returns namely, fixity of land and capital and technology are destroyed by the dynamic forces 
of growth, namely additions to the capital stock progress in techniques of production and 
improvements in the skills of labor.  
Efficiency in growth 
While growth is on or output is increasing, it is essential to ensure efficiency in the use of 
resources. This makes for minimum costs in terms of the use of factors of production. This can 
be achieved through such an allocation and reallocation of resources as it can take the economy 
through changes that are necessary for efficient growth. For example, to promote such a 
production it is necessary that at every stage of growth old industries and old techniques fade 
out and new industries and new techniques be ushered in. Similarly, product mix should 
continuously change to meet the changing requirements of the growing economy. For example, 
with rising incomes of the people consumption pattern changes with a lesser percentage of the 
expenditure on cereals and other food items and larger percentage of expenditure on durable 
goods like TV, motor cars etc. Similarly, raw materials needs of industries undergo change.  
STABILTY IN GROWTH 
For growth to be sustained over long periods it is necessary also to provide for demand for the 
output. Without this growth process can break down. For example, at macro level this involves 
maintaining aggregate demand in line with the rising output.  This boils down to ensuring 
investment corresponding to saving alongside the balance between the demand for and the 
supply of consumer goods. In the market economy this objective is pursued through 
movements in market prices and appropriate monetary and fiscal policies. in a planned 
economy the balancing is done ex-ante in the plans.  
         Thus, economies grow with the expansion in growth – forces associated with capital 
technology and human skill. growth is efficient if resources are collected / reallocated 

--- PAGE 30 ---
corresponding to changes necessary for further increase in production and for higher levels of 
consumption. growth is stable with adequate demand forthcoming to balance the supply of 
goods and services.  
STRUCTURAL CHANGES 
Along with growth in income development is associated with changes in the structure of 
growing economies. These changes transform major aspects of these economies such as 
productive capacity and national income by industrial origin pattern of employment and 
composition of trade. These in turn show themselves in the levels and distribution of incomes 
as also in the consumption patterns of the people. Together these indicate that these countries 
are shedding off the characteristics of backwardness and are in the process of climbing higher 
levels of development.  
INCREASE IN PRODUCTIVE CAPACITY 
A change of basic importance is the increase in the productive capacity of the country. This 
takes place because of two developments. One relates to the stock of physical capital. Since 
with increase in per capita income, saving – rate is raised it becomes possible to plough an 
increasing amount of resources into capital goods like, buildings, roads, machines etc. second 
is the improvement in human capital. This is made possible with availability of large facilities 
for education, research and training. This results in the upgradation of labor skills, advancement 
on the scientific and technological fronts and modernization of people’s attitudes.  
Productive capacity expands also to encompass institutional set ups of the country experiencing 
growth. In fact, while increase in physical capital provides wherewithal for the institutional set-
up the increase in human capital provides knowledge and personnel for growth – promoting 
institutions. These institutions span many activities like collection and disbursement of labor 
resources etc. the relevant institutions take on the forms of banks, investment – houses, joint – 
stock companies, stock exchanges etc.  
PROGRESSIVE PRODUCTION STRUCTURE 
With growth sustained over long periods production structure undergoes radical changes in 
several respects. One such aspect is national income by industrial origin. W It is for the simple 
reason that most of the economy’s growth is caused by the increase in industrial output. This 
happens because industries are subject to higher productivity increases due to such factors as 
the operations of increasing returns. Another major area affected is the pattern of employment. 
The proportion of working force engaged in non-agricultural sectors increases tremendously 
whereas in agricultural sector it falls equally tremendously. Another aspect that undergoes big 
changes is the composition of foreign trade of the country. In exports industrial goods begin to 
form a major proportion. This is because the rapidly expanding supplies of industrial goods 
seek foreign demand in addition to domestic demand. In imports of raw materials and other 
goods, wherein the country has less comparative advantages, start figuring prominently. All 
these changes mark advances of the economy towards higher levels of development.

HIGHER LIVING AND REDUCED INEQUALITY 
The transformation of the economy induces permanent changes in the living of the people. 
These take the form of higher standards of consumption and lessening income inequalities. 
This far-reaching implications for the economic and social life of the country. The high per 
capita income is a sure guarantee of a high saving rate and as a consequence a high investment 
rate. The high income also ensures a consumption pattern with cereals and other food items 
very low in the expenditure scale and comforts and luxuries very high in the scale. At the high-
income stage, income inequalities cease to be as large as these are at the low-income stage of 
development. Even if the degree of inequalities is the same in both the high- and low-income 
stages of development, the misery and tensions associated with inequalities are far less at the 
developed stage. The reason is that at the developed stage even the poor have sufficient to meet 
their necessities as also some comforts.  
      Structural changes thus signify that the economy is a progressive one sustained growth over 
the long period and structural changes go hand in hand pointing to the development of the 
economy.

and considerations contribute to growth may be detailed upon. 
Natural resources: consisting of climate, soil, rainfall, mineral deposits and sources of power, 
these provide the natural base and constitute the fundamental factor in the capacity of a country 
to grow. To an extent these can be augmented by international trade, but all resources are not 
tradeable. However, despite their general fixity or scarcity their availability can be increased. 
Such an increase can be visualized in several ways. One, there are resources which can be 
renewed with proper conservation practices. Arable land, pastureland and timber land are some 
of the examples of resources that can be used again. There are two resources that can be added. 
for example, there exist deposits which are not known. when they discovered these augments 
the supply of natural resources. Similarly with irrigation double or Trible cropping becomes 
possible. This adds to the cultivated area. Three, increase in quantity and improvement in 
quality of these resources have been made possible by technological advance. for, example new 
techniques have led to greater economy in the use of scarce resources. Further, more efficient 
acquisition of resources has resulted in lower cost and greater supplies. Again, substitutes like 
synthetics have caused saving of scarce resources. Natural resources are thus flexible in 
supplies despite their scarcity.  
 

--- PAGE 32 ---
HUMAN RESCOURES  
The size and quality of labor are of vital importance in determining the productive capacity. 
The size is relevant in providing labor force to work with capital and on natural resources. 
Generally, a growing size should be helpful. But in a given situation there is an optimum 
number that ensures the highest average productivity. Beyond that number a falling marginal 
product raises the national product at a lower rate and lowers the average productivity of 
workers. Thus, an increase in population is not always a blessing.  
        Quality of population depends upon its health, vigor, education, training, morale etc. 
provision of pure drinking water, medical facilities, education and training opportunities etc. 
are tantamount to investment in human capital as distinguished from investment in physical 
capital like machines, tools etc. It has been estimated that the return in terms of output has been 
as high or even higher from human capital than from an equal investment in physical capital. 
This conclusion is becoming increasingly valid with the advancement of technology and 
sophistication in products. The educated trained and alert labor force is very essential to man 
the complicated machines and to manage the complex economic life of growing economies.  
CAPITAL FORMATION 
The capital stock of a country determines in a large measure how many laborers of that capable 
of producing. Real capital per worker shows its output – capacity regardless of the skill of the 
workers. As such capital stock is of crucial formation. In fact, it is this stock again which 
conditions the growth of human capital in terms of the building, equipment, books etc. which 
makes available to educational and training institutes. Again, the indirect or round about 
production which capital goods make possible is a basic means to enhance productive 
efficiency.  
Of course, the size of output associated with capital depends upon the capital output ratio i.e. 
the relationship between net investment and the resulting increase in production. If for example 
this ratio is 2:1 then every two rupees of net investment in year 1 makes the economy capable 
of producing one of additional output in year two and succeeding years. This ratio depends 
upon the pattern of investment and technology. for example, in a heavy industry like steel with 
a high capital-intensive technology the capital output ratio is considerable. On the other hand, 
in light consumer industries with low capital intensity output per unit of capital is much higher. 
Thus, given a pattern of development with technology which could be varied within limits, a 
larger capital stock should enable a country to secure a larger output. From this it follows that 
for growth to proceed it is necessary that an increasing amount of resources should be used for 
building capital stock.  
TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCE 
Technical progress that is turning out to be a better product at the same cost or the same product 
at lower cost or both contributes to the increase in output. New knowledge of production 
methods gets embodied in new machines and new equipment capable of producing more goods 
or new goods. As an illustration a country may every year produce enough capital goods to 
replace the existing worn-out capital stock, i.e sufficient to equal depreciation. in this case 

--- PAGE 33 ---
output capacity remains the same year. Suppose however that there is growth of knowledge so 
that as the equipment wears out it is replaced by different and more productive equipment. In 
this case national output will grow because of knowledge rather than because of the 
accumulation of more capital.  
While technical knowledge is an independent factor there is no doubt about the fact that capital 
formation and technical advance are closely related processes. The development and 
application of new products or new productive techniques typically entail investment in new 
machines and equipment. But the idea behind the technical advance that there are more efficient 
ways of doing things has its distinct place in the production profile of a country. This idea can 
be robbed at home more effectively by referring to an example where no additional capital and 
in fact no capital is involved. Modern crop rotation practices and contour ploughing, for 
example, contribute greatly to output although they do not necessarily entail the use of more 
capital equipment.  
ENSURING FULL CAPACITY- UTILIZATION 
Besides the four factors namely natural resources, capital formation and technological advance, 
bearing on the supply side of the growth – process there are two additional considerations to 
be kept in view, one is the need to ensure that the existing capacity is fully utilized. Otherwise, 
national output will be less than could be possible. To avoid underutilization of capacity it is 
necessary to maintain aggregate demand at the level of full employment of productive capacity. 
This boils down to the necessity of seeing that the expenditure on consumer goods matches the 
supply of consumer goods and that increase in productive capacity or investment equals saving. 
In case of raising investment is not matched by rising saving consumption expenditure may 
outstrip consumption goods resulting in an inflationary rise in prices and thus destabilizing the 
economy. in a market economy monetary and fiscal policies are used. in a planned economy 
the same aim can be pursued by providing ex-ante in plans the required division of total 
incomes meant for consumption and for saving.  
EFFICIENT PRODUTION  
The second consideration is to ensure efficient production through proper allocation of 
resources. This involves two steps. One is related to the allocation of resources on the 
production side of the growth process. When a country is growing there are some industries 
which become obsolete just as some workers’ skills become out of date. New industries take 
their place requiring new skills. To avoid wastages and quicker changeover from the old to the 
new, it is necessary number of resources get allocated.  
The second step concerns the change in the economic structure to suit the changing pattern of 
consumption. With rise in income growth, it makes possible the package of consumption goods 
that people consume undergoes change. Beyond a certain level of income, the proportion of 
expenditure on food items falls and that on non-food items like consumer durables increases. 
To meet the changing pattern of consumption structure of industries producing consumer goods 
as also those supplying inputs to them must change. Otherwise, production will be less 
efficient, for the non-conformity of industrial structure to the changing consumption patterns 
may result in the non-utilization of some resources.  

--- PAGE 34 ---
APPROPRIATE ENVIRONMENT 
Broadly this pertains to the agencies that organize resources for growth and the attitudes of the 
people towards economic activities. Organizing agencies, namely, government, business 
leadership, labor leadership can promote growth seeking. A good government can for instance 
frame suitable policies, prepare right kind of plans, create opportunities for entrepreneurial 
abilities to flower etc. It can also make production relations pro-growth by changing land 
tenurial system creation of infrastructural facilities etc. it can help growth by promoting 
institutions to mobilize finances and channel investments in the desired directions. Business 
leaders with drive can break new grounds in products, techniques in markets etc. A growth – 
prone labor leadership may regard boosting production as important an objective as sharing of 
the output.  
 No less important are the attitudes of the people towards work earnings and spending. These 
can promote development if these are based on economic rationale i.e, desiring more work for 
more income for more expenditure and for more saving. A community that respects hard work 
and prides on honesty has a consciousness favorable for rapid progress.  
      Growth thus requires factors like natural and human resources, capital formation and 
technological advance. It is alco necessary that the productive capacity is fully utilized 
production is efficient and the agencies and people’s attitudes are pro-growth.  
MEASURES FOR DEVELOPMENT 
In uplifting a backward -looking low level economy to a high -level progressive economy 
efforts of various sorts have to be made. We may explain the same under the following heads.  
Increasing capital formation: since growth or increase in output is the basic requirement for 
raising incomes of the people, it is necessary that the supplies of factors bearing on production 
are increased. One and perhaps the most important factor is capital stock. Both physical and 
human. Physical stock increase will mean more capital per worker than at present. This will 
enable the workers to produce more, which in turn will raise their productivity and income. 
This requires that the saving rate of the economy is stepped up substantially from the present 
low rate so that the rate of capital formation can be raised significantly. Indias present saving 
rate for example is in the range of 20-24 per cent of the gross domestic product (GDP). This 
needs to be raised to around 30 per cent to make a worthwhile impact on the capital stock of 
the country. To the extent it is not possible to do so in the short period of a few years, foreign 
capital may be sought. of the two forms of capital namely, debt and equity the direct investment 
should be encouraged. It brings with it advanced expertise and most modern technologies.  
   Improving human capital: Another component of capital stock of a country is the human 
capital. It helps in raising production, but more importantly it is essential for the development 
of innovative technologies. Apart from the highly educated and trained personnel, it is also 
important that the knowledge and skill -level of the mass of the people are raised. As has been 
proved by the experiences of the highly industrialized countries, this strengthens the base of 
the economy, which in turn quickness the growth rate and raises the efficiency and quality of 
products. In India for example apart from increasing the highly skilled personnel, there is 

--- PAGE 35 ---
comparatively a greater need for rising the literacy level of the masses because almost half of 
the population is illiterate. in fact, in the case of the large many in the working age (15to 65) 
the health status also needs to be improved much to make them physically fit as producers.
